speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT NEAVSPAPER COMMENT ON SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. My attention has been drawn to an article appearing on the front page of the Montreal Gazette under date of February 6, of this year. The article is headed:
Compromise in School Rates is Suggested
Below that appears the sub-heading:
Provincial Liberals Object to Criticism of Tasehereau by J. F. Pouliot, M.P.
I have a few comments to make on this article, so I intend to take it up paragraph by paragraph, and it begins as follows:
Special to the Gazette. Quebec, February 4: For the present at least it is not intended to name a commission to revise the Quebec municipal code. The last revision was approved by the legislature in 1915-
That is wrong; it was done in 1916.
-and amendments to the Municipal Code are not very frequent.
This is another mistake, because inside of ten years two hundred amendments have been made to the eight hundred articles of the code.
Premier Tasehereau is not suffering from a lack of offers to revise the code, and only recently answered in the negative to a request of Jean-Francois Pouliot, Liberal M.P. for Temiscouata, that he be appointed to undertake the work.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT NEAVSPAPER COMMENT ON SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT NEAVSPAPER COMMENT ON SPEECH IN THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Well, Sir, to satisfy hon.
members on both sides of the house, I will tell them now that I have nothing offensive to say about Mr. Tasehereau to-day, and I will make my reply to this article as short as possible. First I would like to know if there is some expert or artist in quotations in the department of the Attorney General of Quebec who subtilizes documents in file and falsifies texts? I do not believe there is. I rather believe it comes from the correspondent of the Gazette in Quebec, who is the janitor of the falsehood factory or Ananias club of Quebec, and if such a thing happens once more I will name him so that the country will know the fellow as he is. I received only one letter from Mr. Tasehereau in that connection, and I will read to the house that section of the letter in connection with this article. The municipalities association of Quebec asked the

Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
government to make a new draft of the Quebec municipal code because of the very many amendments which had been made, and I wrote telling Mr. Taschereau that if he wanted me to act as commissioner for this purpose I would gratefully accept. That part of the report is true, but my letter was written a long time before the house opened; it was written on November 4, while Mr. Taschereau was giving interviews to the papers in Ottawa during the Dominion-provincial conference. I received his answer when he went back to Quebec, and I will read the French text, which I shall be glad to show any hon. member of the house, and I hope Mr. Taschereau will not deny his signature. On November 12th ult., he acknowledges receipt of my letter of November 4, and the last paragraph of his letter reads as follows:
Je ne manquerai pas, au cours de la prochaine session, de faire part a la chambre de votre proposition.
I will translate that into English for the benefit of my English-speaking friends, and I wonder if they will take it as an affirmative or a negative answer. No one will change this letter, because I keep it in a steel file. The last paragraph is as follows:
I will not fail during the next session to submit your proposition to the legislative assembly.
Contrary to Esau, who sold his birthright for a mess of pottage, I have no hesitation in saying that if I have to choose between a job offered by any government, any company or any individual, and freedom of speech, I will always choose freedom of speech.
Now I crave the indulgence of the house to read further from this article, which is as malicious as it is slanderous, not only against myself but against every member of this house from the province of Quebec.
The attack which Mr. Pouliot made upon Premier Taschereau in his speech in the House of Commons had aroused considerable feeling here.-*
This I did not expect.
-and _ especially the statement that the provincial Liberals have regard for their federal brothers only when there is a provincial election. Provincial Liberals maintain that such is not the case, but if anything the situation has been the reverse. The Liberals have been in power at Quebec since 1897, which has meant handling of considerable patronage, and during the dark ten years, from 1911 to 1921, when the federal Liberals were out of power this patronage had to be spread so as to care for the victims of 1911,-
I was not one of them; do I look like a victim?
-and at times the butter was very thin,
There was no question of Australian butter at that time.
-and there was no jam whatever owing to the care bestowed upon the federal Liberals.
My answer to that is that the young man who wrote that article is known as a buffoon in Quebec. His bread is well buttered, and I am sure that he is jammed with that well buttered bread. The article goes on to say:
Provincial judgeships, positions as crown prosecutors-
I am not a judge, I am not a crown prosecutor.
-and other positions have been handed out by the Quebec Liberal government to distressed federal friends-
He should name them.
-and it has always been the provincial Liberal organization which has furnished the fighting means at federal elections-
I never knew that.
-not to mention the fact that the two official Liberal organs in the province receive their government support from Quebec, and not from Ottawa.
I draw that statement to the attention of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and of the Finance minister (Mr. Robb).
Hence, provincial Liberals who have had to make way for the needs of federal Liberals fail to appreciate the attack made by Mr. Pouliot on Premier Taschereau.
I hope the house will allow me to answer that by a little story. When I was at college an elderly cousin of mine called on me the first year I was a boarder, and brought me once a bag of six very small strawberry tartlets. During the following summer she called at our house and when she found I was not very polite to her she said: "Why are you so impolite when I fed you last year?" Mr. Speaker, I have just a word more to add and it is this: I do not believe that false, malicious, slanderous story comes from Mr. Taschereau because I think he is enough of a gentleman to take the responsibility of what he says. But whomsoever it comes from I say to him that I despise a man who will make such insinuations. If Mr. Taschereau is not satisfied with what I have said, let him produce and lay on the table of the Quebec legislative assembly the official correspondence that has taken place between us since 1921.

The house resumed from Tuesday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.
The Address-Mr. Veniot

Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I desire at the very outset to extend my personal congratulations' to the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Bennett). Some hon. members from the west told this house that they felt proud he had been chosen, because the great Conservative party had to go to the west to find a leader. I wish to say to our friends from the west who spoke in that way that we in the maritime provinces are very jealous of the honours that come to us, and that we cannot allow the west to take all the credit in regard to the choice made of the leader of the opposition. The hon. gentleman, I regret to say, is not in his seat at the present moment. I should like to see him there because I, as one New Bruns-wicker, would like to extend my personal congratulations to him as another New Brunswicker. It was in that province that he saw the light of day although, it is true, in one of its smallest counties. But coming from that small county, as he does, he occupies to-day the greatest position in the gift of the party to which he has adhered for so many years. I as a New Brunswicker feel proud of the faot that one of the great political parties in this country has chosen a native of my province to lead it and to help it in shaping its course for the future.
I have only forty minutes at my disposal, and I have certain important points which I wish to lay before the house. Therefore as regards the gentlemen who moved and seconded the address I will merely repeat what has been well said already as to the splendid way in which they discharged their duties. Not only do I congratulate them, but I hope they will long live to enjoy the position they now hold in the hearts of the people who have sent them here as their representatives.
I would not have spoken on the address, Mr. Speaker, had it not been that certain members from the maritime provinces have thought fit to cast doubt upon some statements I made at two meetings, one at Amherst, Nova Scotia and the other at St. John, N.B., in relation to what is known as "maritime rights", a subject now worn pretty nearly threadbare. Doubt having been cast upon the statements I made on those occasions I wished to take the very earliest opportunity to prove to this house that I was correct when I said that there were only ten direct recommendations made in the Duncan, report, and it is beyond doubt that there were only ten such direct recommendations, putting to one side suggestions and expressions of feeling on the part of the com-

mission, as well as arguments advanced by those who presented themselves before the commission. I make that statement now and I defy honest contradiction of it. Out of those ten direct recommendations, eight were implemented to the extent that it was practicable to implement them by legislation, by the various departments of the government, leaving two recommendations yet to be implemented and which, I understand, are to-day receiving the consideration of the government. Having made the statement that there were only ten direct recommendations, I intend to deal with those recommendations, and to show to the house the propaganda that has been instituted in the maritime provinces by certain persons. I am not going to attribute any motives to these persons, but I am going to lay the facts before the house and let the house come to a decision thereon. I remind hon. members of the action taken by parliament, and by this government last winter, of the consideration shown to the claims of the maritime provinces by our friends from the west, from Ontario, from Quebec, and from British Columbia. On that occasion all joined hands in an endeavour to obtain redress of the wrongs, so-claimed, of the maritimes; and in view of that action it is humiliating to think that to-day certain people in the maritime provinces are attempting to make a political football of what has already been done, and what may yet remain to be done, in connection with this important question. Is it any wonder that there is doubt in the minds of the people from the other provinces, who stood so loyally by the maritimes last winter as to whether we were sincere or not? Is there any wonder that some of those from other provinces who cooperated with us may entertain a feeling that we in the maritime provinces can never be satisfied? Is it any wonder that those of us on both sides of this house who have been advocating those rights-and I wish to give credit to our Conservative friends for the manner in which they stood by my colleague in the government and myself on this question-have, within the last two or three months, heard rumours that it is impossible to satisfy the maritime provinces?
Let me take up the first recommendation of the Duncan report in regard to the money grants to the provinces. That recommendation has been implemented to the full. Every suggestion made in the recommendation has been carried out. Let me correct the statement of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) that the extra subsidy was not paid

The Address-Mr. Veniot
to the Nova Scotia government during the session of parliament of last year. How could it be paid then? Why does the hon. member wish to leave the impression that the government of this country was keeping back that payment? The hon. gentleman should know that a certain practice prevails which regulates the payment of subsidies. These subsidies are paid twice a year on the first of July and the first of January, and on the first of July of last year a cheque was sent to the public treasury of Nova Scotia. If, as the hon. gentleman states, anything was kept back of money due to Nova Scotia by this government, that money was kept, not out of the extra subsidy, but out of the regular subsidy that was due Nova Scotia. That shows how the false impression was created and spread about, causing dissatisfaction.
Was it not the recommendation of the Duncan commission that the amount of $875,000 should be paid forthwith?

I was coming to that. The
hon. gentleman has now given me the very ammunition I want and I thank him for doing so. There is another attempt on the part of somebody to leave the impression that the government of this country are tardy in paying this amount because the Duncan commission used the word "forthwith." Of course it did but parliament had to vote the money. The money could not be paid forthwith without a vote of this house and it could not be paid by the government until parliament voted it.

Why did the government
not get the vote?

We did not forget to vote
it. The hon. gentleman himself took a part in that vote. But the money could not be paid until the sanction of the proper authority in the person of the Governor General of this Dominion had been obtained and he had signed the act making it imperative upon the federal government to pay over these subsidies. What are the facts? This house rose late in the month of April of last year, and after the business of the house had been cleaned up and royal sanction had been given to all the bills that had been passed, this amount was paid on the first of July. On the 17th November, within seven months after the prorogation of parliament, the second amount was paid. The government did not wait to carry out the usual practice and pay the money only on the first of January. My hon. friend did not state that
to the house and those who are using that argument are using it like the chairman of the board of trade of the city of Saint John, who used that argument at a meeting on the sixth day of December in that city. The Premier of New Brunswick who was sitting by his side allowed that statement to go without contradiction, or at least no contradiction appeared in the report, when he knew that that amount had been paid to New Brunswick four weeks prior to the date that the chairman was addressing the board of trade in that city. That is a sample of the propaganda which is circulated throughout the maritime provinces in connection with the Duncan report.
Lot me come now to transportation and freight rates. A great deal has been said in regard to the question of transportation and the reduction of freight rates. It has been stated and the statement has been circulated broadcast by the boards of trade of Halifax and Saint John, the Saint John Telegraph-Journal and the Premier of New Brunswick, that the general average reduction was only sixteen per cent. I have in my possession a return which I asked for and received yesterday from the railway commission. The reason I asked for this return was because I wished to place it before the house. It shows the work done in checking up the twenty per cent reduction given by the Canadian National Railways from the first day of July to the pres-emt moment, and I am going to ask the permission of the house to place that return on the record because, as it is rather lengthy, it would take too much of the forty minutes at my disposal to read it. This, however, is what it will contain:

I ask the hon. senior member for the city of Saint John (Mr. MacLaren) to pay par-
The Address-Mr. Veniol

ticular attention to this, and to study these figures carefully when they appear in Hansard to-morrow. He will see that the reduction was not sixteen per cent. -

I made no statement
in reference to any percentage.

I did not say that the hon. gentleman did. I asked him to study the figures and he will see that the reduction was not sixteen per cent, but more. The reason why I am calling his attention to this is because the propaganda on the sixteen per cent reduction originated in the city of Saint John, the home city of my hon. friend. As I have known him now for a number of years to be honest and conscientious in anything he wishes to advance, I feel sure that when he finds out that the statement advanced by the board of trade, of which I believe he is a member, the Saint John Telegraph-Journal and the Premier of New Brunswick, is not right, he will be honest enough to stand up in public in the city of Saint John at the first opportunity and point out that those gentlemen were wrong and that I was right.
I would wish for a ruling of the railway commission which I shall be pleased to accept.

Yet in the face of that the Saint John board of trade, on the word of a so-called freight expert, sends out to the world the statement that the Canadian National have refused to comply with the orders of the railway commission and that all that we are getting today is a 16 per cent reduction.
Let me call the attention of the hon. senior member for the city of Saint John to a state-
The Address-Mr. Veniot

ment which he made yesterday and which is not in accordance with the facts. The hon. gentleman, if I mistake not-and if I am wrong I know he will correct me-stated that the Canadian National Railways had submitted a freight schedule to the railway commission and that the railway commission had returned it to them with orders to revise their schedule to give a 20 per cent reduction. I want to say now-and I am not saying this in contradiction of the hon. gentleman personally because I believe that he was mis-[DOT] informed and got this so-called information through the instrumentality of the Saint John board of trade-that that statement is absolutely false. I make that statement boldly because within ten minutes after the hon. gentleman made his statement on the floor of this house, I called up the railway commission and quoted him verbatim and 'in reply the railway commission said, No. As a proof of the fact that the hon. gentleman's statement is not correct, let me say that we are now using that very same schedule to check up all the freight carrying of the Canadian National Railways in order to see if their schedules come within the twenty per cent reduction as recommended by the Duncan report, and so far we find that they do.
May I ask if the tariffs of the Canadian National Railways have yet been approved by the railway commission?

I did not say they had
been. I said that the railway commission have the schedules that were submitted on July 1, 1927, and that they are checking them up, and that checking shows the percentages that I show here. When they are through checking them up it will be found, I am positive, that the same ratio or proportion of reduction will be carried right down through the whole schedules as submitted to be effective July 1, 1927.

You will add jam to the
bread and butter.

It would be better if the
hon. gentleman would add some sense to his interjections.

Very parliamentary language for a
minister.

There is another gentleman from the eastern provinces who is feeling the shoe pinch.
Dealing with the question of freight rates and the figures I am submitting to the house, I wish to say that it is not a question of paper reductions such as are being asked for

by certain so-called freight rate experts independent of the volume moving, but it is the percentage reduction of traffic as it actually moves over the line. In the case of a general reduction, the percentage reduction of the traffic as it actually moves is the only real test of what has been done, and the figures I have given are no paper reduction but represent the actual reduction calculated on the quantity of freight moved over the line in comparison with the quantity moved over the line previously at a higher rate. No better criterion can be found or accepted.
Let me go further. The third paragraph deals with port development and export. This question is divided into four sections dealing respectively with Canadian trade, Canadian ports, statutory harbour commissions, port development, maritime trade and harbour facilities. So far as this recommendation of the Duncan report is concerned, it has been carried out by the establishment of the harbour commissions. I know that certain persons in Nova Scotia maintain that Halifax should be put upon the basis of an absolutely national port and should not be called upon to pay any revenue or meet any of the expenses incumbent upon the development of that port in the way of interest, and so forth. The people of St. John have accepted the Duncan report, have accepted the commission, and are prepared to do their share in carrying on the affairs of that harbour, and to meet so far as possible the amounts necessary to pay interest on the capital that will be expended in the greater development of the port of St. John. Halifax is no better than St. John.
While I am not going to refer at all to the attitude that the people of Halifax assumed up to a certain period, let me say that Halifax finally has accepted the action of this government in implementing the Duncan report, and I am proud to learn that they are going on working out that recommendation, and I hope, and dearly hope, that both St. John and Halifax will in the very near future become great grain-exporting ports of the Dominion of Canada. That is the end to which we Should work, and' so long as I have a voice in the affairs of this Dominion, so long as I have the honour to occupy a seat in this house-
It will not be long.

You cannot knock us out.
My hon. friend is whistling to keep his courage up. So long as I occupy a seat in this house, and I expect to occupy my seat long after my hon. friend is politically dead, I shall put forth my very 'best efforts, whether I succeed or not, and I feel I shall succeed, in helping

The Address-Mr. Veniot
to build up the ports of the maritime provinces, and not only to carry out all that the Duncan commission recommends, but as the years go 'by and the trade of Canada grows, the government of this country will have an eye to it that St. John and Halifax will come into their own. I have confidence in the government and Prime Minister of this country. The Prime Minister stated from his place in the house last session what the government intended to do, and he said that he would carry out what he had stated. I had absolute faith in him when he made that statement, and he has done nothing since that would tend to shake that faith no matter by whom held.
Now I come to the trade policy. What do we find? The Duncan report recommended that the Dominion government should apply its mind to this proposition in the light of maritime province interests and having regard also to the position of other provinces concerned with these same products-that is, the basic products of the maritime provinces, the products of the forest and of the sea-with a view to entering into closer trade relations with the United States so that the products of the forest and of the fishing industry would be allowed to enter the American market on reciprocal terms.
Our friends of the opposition have been attempting, either in this house or in the country, to condemn the present government, saying that we have been inactive in that respect. Would it not make anyone smile, Mr. Speaker, to hear a Conservative blaming a Liberal government because they did not get down on their knees every day in the week, and twice on Sunday, pleading with the Americans to give reciprocity to Canada? Our friends are not consistent. The Prime Minister in laying before this house the program which the government intended to follow in regard to these recommendations pointed out that there is to-day, and always has been under Liberal rule, a clause in the tariff which gives power to the Governor General in Council to enter into reciprocal negotiations with the United States in regard to natural products, and the gentleman who went before the Duncan commission and asked that we enter into closer reciprocal trade relations with the United States was no less a gentleman than the Prime Minister of New Brunswick, the Hon. Mr. Baxter, the one who led the phalanx in 1911 when we were trying to get reciprocity with the United States and who went up and down New Brunswick telling the people that it was disloyal to have any truck or trade with the Yankees. Perhaps I will be pardoned if I say that that is the class of political bunkum 56103-is
that hon. gentlemen are interested in, and that is being spread as propaganda throughout the length and breadth of the maritime provinces.
Like Moses Asiz.

What did the hon. member say? He never opens his mouth that he does not put his foot in it.
Now I come to category 4 of this recommendation, respecting the coking plant. I am not going to discuss at length the question of the coking plant. The Duncan commission recommended certain things and the government have implemented this recommendation to the full. An attempt may be made to state otherwise, because the government has not yet dealt with the coal duty to protect Canadian coal. Be that as it may, the Duncan report in that respect has been implemented.
Then we go on and take the question of the bounty on steel. The recommendation so far as the bounty on steel is concerned, has not been implemented. At the very moment the Duncan report was being prepared by this house the tariff board was considering the question of the bounty on steel. The Duncan report recommended that they should also deal with the question of the duty on coal and the tariff board have this question now before them.
Having dealt with these recommendations which pertain particularly to Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, let me say that I intended to deal with the recommendations that pertain to Prince Edward island, but my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Sinclair) in a well thought out speech, in a speech consisting of strong arguments, pointed out how the government had fully implemented the Duncan report, so far as Prince Edward Island was concerned. I said a few minutes ago that propaganda was started in New Brunswick in order to belittle what has been done under the Duncan report. Let me give you an example. I hold in my hand an extract from the St. John Telegraph-Journal dated October 14, and this is what I find:

Mr. Speaker, it is not my purpose to impose on the mover (Mr. Ilsley) and the seconder (Mr. Beaubien) of the address any formal congratulation, but just in passing I should like to wish them the compliments of the session, and save time that way. We often hear a great deal about the prosperity of Canada, and it is true that we are enjoying a certain amount of prosperity. Why not? We have perhaps one of the richest countries in the world in natural resources, one of the richest per capita to be found anywhere. We have enjoyed in addition to that excellent prices for our basic metals and, until recently, good prices for our timber. We have been blessed with three or four years of good growing conditions and excellent crops, and have been able to place our crops on a market that was *bare in comparison with what it was immediately before the war, largely due to the fact that Russia and some other countries were not producing to the extent that they were before1 the war took place. Then again we have had cheap money available. Money has been getting cheaper as the world has been getting back to normal business conditions, so that we have been able to secure capital for the development of our resources at fairly easy rates. After all, therefore, you cannot attribute this prosperity to the actions of the present government; if the Conservative party had been in power under similar conditions I think our modesty would have prevented us from claiming credit for it. Taking it all in all I think it has been a matter of good luck on the part of the Liberal party rather more than anything else.
The question of our status has occupied a good deal of the time of the house, and I do not propose to trespass on the time of hon. members by discussing the matter at any length; I think there are many other matters in which the rank and file of the Canadian people are more interested. Speaking from my own experience, having lived

The Address-Mr. Tolmie
a little more than half a century on the Pacific coast, I can recall several occasions during that period when it was a very lucky thing indeed that Canada was a part of the British Empire. My experience has led me to think that we should try to get closer to that empire rather than endeavour to see how far out of it we can get and still remain in it. Looking into the future, and having regard to the tremendous development that will take place on the Pacific coast within the next few years, we shall unquestionably find it to our benefit, to be part of and cooperate with the great British Empire, and to learn at the earliest possible moment to do our duty towards that empire and help to carry a part of the heavy burden now almost entirely imposed on the mother country.
I think the matter which has been referred to by one or two of the previous speakers, the emigration of our young men and1 women, is one of the greatest tragedies that we have to face. We educate our young people in our universities and schools at considerable expense, only to find that when they are ready to undertake employment there is no employment offering for them in their own country. We can only keep them at home by offering them equal treatment to that which they will receive in the United States or elsewhere. They must be paid wages just as attractive; they must be given working conditions that are at least just as good, and we must have work offering for them in sufficient volume to engage them when they are ready to undertake it. To-day then we should make the best of our opportunities. We have a country, as I have already pointed out, rich in natural resources, and we Should try to have the Canadian people themselves develop these resources to the fullest possible extent. We have a tariff to use if we wish. I am not one of those who think that the only good we can get out of the tariff is by raising it. In certain cases where a lowering of the tariff would get us more business, by making bargains with other countries and so forth, let us adopt that course. In other cases where a certain amount of protection is necessary, let us apply protection, always using the tariff as an instrument to better the conditions in our country and to keep the work 'here for our own people. We must cut out sectionalism. We must take a country-wide view of the whole situation, a Canadian rather than a provincial or district view. We must keep under consideration all the various activities in this great country of ours, always remembering that conditions are not the same in one part of the country as they are in another, and adopt a system of
give and take, if we are going to build up a united Canada. No one should expect any special treatment in his particular line. We should adopt as a principle the policy of manufacturing our raw products at home to the fullest possible extent, although I fully realize that this cannot be applied in every case- that it cannot be applied to as great an extent as we would like to apply it.
In the matter of wheat, I think we should adopt the principle of putting through the processes of manufacture in Canada every bushel of wheat we possibly can, and selling that product in raw form only where we cannot manufacture at home. Two great advantages would result from this policy, first, the work it would provide for our own people, and second, and almost as important, the retention of the offal, the bran and shorts that are left over after the manufacture of flour, for the use of our live stock men in building up that very important branch of agriculture.
Then in regard to our timber, we should manufacture our woods as much as we possibly can. There are certain conditions under which it pays us better to export timber in the form of logs. There are certain conditions of the market on the Pacific coast under which it would pay us to ship the logs out of the country and receive the cash for them rather than hold them on a slow market and have them injured by the teredo worm or depreciated in value from other causes.
At one time in British Columbia we shipped the bulk of our minerals south of the line to be refined; some went to Wales. Down on the Columbia river below Ross-land, in West Kootenay, we have a little town of eight thousand people, built up entirely by refining our raw ores instead of shipping them away. What has been the result? This town of eight thousand people has been established; the payroll is eight million dollars per year; the refinery require certain other things not directly connected with the refining, making it necessary for them to buy in one single year five thousand tons of structural steel, three and a half million bricks, four and a half mdlion feet of lumber, and one carload of cement every two days throughout the year. They are buying these things in British Columbia and building up a great consuming centre where our farmers and agriculturists can sell their products without paying heavy freight rates to far distant markets. What I want to point out is this, that if we had still continued the old system of shipping out our raw products, we should not be deriving the benefits that I have described.

In my opinion we should remove any inequalities in the tariff which are detrimental to the development of Canada. Particularly do I refer to agricultural products on which in the tariffs between Canada and the United States the balance is in favour of our neighbours. As you know, Mr. Speaker, they are in a very much better position than we are for the production of early produce, such as eggs, vegetables and fruits of various kinds, which they are able to ship into our country against a very low tariff in comparison with that demanded of our shippers in the event of their finding it necessary to market their surplus south of the line.
Let us learn, too, to run Canada for the benefit of the Canadian people first-for those people who stay in the country, who pay our taxes and conduct the government. Take the woollen industry as another illustration of what I have been urging. Our manufacturers have been protected to a certain extent until the woollen industry has reached a production volume of about one hundred million dollars per year. But look at our sheep population. Our farmers receive no protection for their raw wool. What do we find as a result? Australia with a sheep population of ninety-seven million; Great Britain-a small country in area-with over twenty million; little New Zealand with twenty-seven million; the United States with between thirty and forty million-and Canada with only two and three-quarter million. Why? Our wool has never been protected, and we have not had the stabilizing effect that the protection of wool would bring about. Compare this condition with that in the United States. They have a tariff on raw wool running as high in some cases as forty-five cents a pound, with the result that their wool and sheep industry is on a sound basis and is making more and more progress from year to year.
We should encourage the consumption of home products in every way possible. I am a very firm believer in keeping our Canadian dollar circulating in the country as long as we possibly can. I might suggest to the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Cardin), as was pointed out by a previous speaker, that one of the most practical ways of doing this would be to make sure that Canadian coal is burned in government ships. Then, taking into consideration the fact that we are importing from the United States nearly seven hundred million dollars' worth of products every year, and that many of those products could be produced in this country, I think very good results would be obtained by making a careful analysis of

the imports and selecting those particular lines which we can produce here at a profit, and then stimulating and encouraging in every way their production at home instead of importing them from another country.
In this particular connection we might begin on butter almost right away. While I am strongly in favour of cultivating trade within the empire, I do think that the butter-maker of Canada is receiving unfair treatment under present conditions. Even my good friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) I know will admit that it is useless for our dairymen to attempt in the middle of winter the production of butter with stored feed, such as hay, grain, ensilage, and so forth, in competition with the grass butter of New Zealand; but this is what they are up against at this time of the year. It is all nonsense to tell us that the Canadian dairyman was very much delighted with the tariff of one cent per pound on butter coming from Australia and New Zealand; at least, judging by the papers, I do not think there is any evidence of delight on his part in some of the reports that I have seen. I have in my hand a report of a meeting in Toronto, held on November 22 and 23, at which the hon. Minister of Agriculture was present. It is interesting reading:
Hon. W. R. Motherwell, Dominion Minister of Agriculture, met with a rather warm reception from the National Dairy Council of Canada in the King Edward Hotel yesterday, and heard, in no uncertain terms, the council's attitude toward the Australian trade treaty.
The minister came as a speaker, but most of his remarks were devoted to an answer to an address by J. A. Caulder, of Regina, Sask., president of the council, who outlined the whole situation, and told of the effect the treaty had on the dairy industry in Canada.
Mr. Motherwell made a half-hearted defence of the treaty, at best, and advised the members of the council to send a strong deputation to Ottawa to meet the government on the matter.
The Australian treaty, said the president, was put over when we were asleep. We were not awake to its effect on us.
During the winter of 1925-26, there were few ill-effects, and Australia did not benefit through the treaty. The next winter, however, was different. There was the strike in England, which injured our market there, and we found ourselves with an over-supply on our hands.
