Another matter which I think is of vital importance to this country is land settlement and colonization. If Canada needs anything it needs people; proper colonization would go a long way towards solving our railway problems and would assist equally in lowering our taxes, besides giving a great stimulus to inr dustry and putting many acres of valuable land to work. I was rather surprised to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) criticized to some extent because he laid the actual conditions before this house. It was insinuated by my hon. friends opposite that we should adopt a sort of Doctor Coue attitude; that by continually telling ourselves we were prosperous, after a time we should be prosperous. I do not think we need hide anything in this country. We Should lay our cards on the table face up, because there is no worse advertisement for Canada than to have a man come here intending to settle and expecting certain conditions, only to be disappointed. I would tell the settler in the first place that there are many opportunities in Canada, but that if he is to succeed he must, expect to work. I would also make it very clear that there is no room here for the loafer who cannot afford to loaf. The spendid opportunities which exist in this country should be brought to the attention of the capitalist, but it should also be made clear to him that while capital invested intelligently and carefully will bring in good returns, Canada is not by any means fool-proof. We should welcome those who are willing to become Canadians and who will work for the progress of Canada. As far as the question of health goes I certainly agree with the government that we should make our inspections on the other side of the ocean. We have brought about the high standard of health of our animals by the strict application of the regulations of the department, and if it is necessary to insist on the health of imported animals it is all the more necessary for us to insist on the health of the people we bring to this country to lay the foundations for future generations.
Let us look for a moment at conditions in British Columbia. There we have a country larger than Washington, Oregon and; California combined; larger than France and Italy, with Switzerland thrown in, and when it comes to the Alpine scenery of Switzerland, we have enough scenery of a similar character in British Columbia to bury twenty-five Switzerlands and have sufficient left to entertain all the

tourists who come our way. We are very rich in natural resources, particularly in mines. Since the first mine was opened in British Columbia we have produced mineral wealth to the value of $900,000,000, and last year we produced mineral products to the value of $70,000,000. The country is rich from the west shore of Vancouver Island1 to the Alberta boundary, with minerals scattered in various districts between those points, and also from the forty-ninth parallel on the south to the Alaskan boundary on the north. So far as prospecting goes, our country has been merely scratched, and the mines already developed clearly indicate that mining in that province is a sound commercial success. Then again, west of the Rockies we have half of the standing commercial saw timber in the whole of Canada, and timber to the value of $82,000,000 was sold from our province last year. We produced 46 per cent of all the fish produced in Canada last year, and the value of our agricultural production amounted to $71,000,000. In addition to that we have a magnificent climate, and we have our splendid ports open the year round, unhampered by frost or ice. In addition to that we are very well located from a geographical standpoint, having easy access to the hundreds of millions of people on the other side of the Pacific, and having access also to the Atlantic side of this continent and to the ports of Europe through the Panama canal. British Columbia is about the same age as the states of Washington and Oregon, and is very little younger than the state of California as far as settlement is concerned. One would think that under these conditions we Should have people flocking to British Columbia in thousands and tens of thousands, looking for an opportunity to locate. But what is the actual situation? While the three states to the south of us can boast of a population of 5J millions, we have but 550,000 people in the whole province of British Columbia. To show you how we are developing in comparison with some of these states, let me say that there are 160 million acres of range lands, and we are using 6 per cent of those lands at the present time, while the state of Washington is using 69.7 per cent of lands of the same character. We are importing 75 per cent of the meat that we require in that province, while the state of Washington is supplying her own meat and exporting the balance to other states. We used 12j million pounds of butter last year in British Columbia. We purchased 7i million pounds outside of the province, producing only 5 million pounds at home. These conditions show the absolute necessity of settlement. in

The Address-Mr. Lovie
that great province bordering on the Pacific ocean. The opportunities there for development are very great indeed, and as I pointed out, the settlement of these lands will bring about such a condition of prosperity as we have not enjoyed up to the present time.
Then with regard to the return of the railway lands to British Columbia: I am pleased to know that the commissioner gave a favourable judgment in connection with this matter, and that the government has intimated in the speech from the throne its desire to return those lands to the province. When British Columbia entered confederation in 1871 one of the provisions was that a railway should be constructed across this country to the Pacific coast, and there was a strong desire on the part of the British government at that time to have connection with their eastern settlements on the Asiatic side of the Pacific. British Columbia not only gave a grant of forty miles of land along the railway, twenty on each side of the line, but contributed in the ordinary way towards the construction of this great road. At that time apparently it was not realized what a great national project it would be; in fact it was stated that the line would never pay for the axle grease used in its operation and that the whole resources of the British Empire could never build and maintain the road. Well, you all know how absurd that prediction was. The railway has turned out to be one of the greatest national projects for the development of Canada that has ever been completed in its history. The Canadian Pacific railway was the pioneer across the prairies of the west. It has developed those great stretches of country, has contributed in no small degree to the growth of British Columbia, and has brought prosperity to Canada as a whole. Under those conditions we in British Columbia feel that being the only province in the whole Dominion which contributed land to that great national highway it is only fair that those lands which were given in trust for the purpose of building that railway should be returned to us now that the enterprise is finished and has accomplished so much. This policy has been pressed by the Conservative party ever since the year 1891.
I sincerely hope that before the end of the session the government will give us an intimation of what it proposes to do in the matter of railway communication into the great Peace river country, connecting that vast rich area with some point on the Pacific coast. This is something that will be looked forward to with great interest by all the people located on the Pacific.
There is one other matter I wish to refer to before taking my seat, and that is the necessity of building good roads throughout this country. Since the advent of the automobile the building of roads is a much more serious proposition than it has been in the past. Roads require to be widened. They must have better surfaces than ever before, be much straighter, possess fewer curves, and so forth. All these requirements tend to make road building much more expensive than it was in former years. The Dominion government after all is a very large user of our roads. The Post Office department, of course, uses our roads daily; in fact every department uses the roads more or less during the year. I should like to suggest to the government that no more popular move could be made than the adoption of the policy brought into effect by the Conservative party in 1919 and kept in operation until 1924, under which certain grants were made to the various provinces in proportion to population. That legislation was much appreciated by all the provinces, and was taken advantage of to the fullest possible extent. These improved highways are necessary to automobiles, and we must remember that the auto truck has come into use to an enormous extent within recent years. Any move therefore, along this line would be warmly welcomed by the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make a few remarks in this debate I congratulate the government upon the fact that it is able to announce in the first paragraph of the speech from the throne that Canada is prosperous. Trade returns all bear out that contention and so far in this debate nothing has been brought forward to controvert the fact.
Certain parts of the prairie provinces have been visited with an epidemic of rust, something that is getting all too common, and the results of which are disastrous to field crops. The crop of the year 1927, although large in the aggregate has not a high money value on account of much of it being low grade, due largely to the ravages of rust. In the province of Manitoba the oat crop was promising but it was practically a failure due to the rust epidemic, and oats both for seed and feed purposes will have to be purchased. For this state of affairs we do not blame the government as they have no control over climatic conditions. On the contrary we give the Minister of Agriculture and his department credit for the amount of research work already accomplished along the line of developing rust resistant strains of

The Address-Mr. Lovie

wheat. I would say, however, that what has been accomplished with respect to agricultural research has hardly touched the fringe of the question, and far more strenuous efforts will have to be made, and more money spent upon agricultural research work if results comparable with the importance of the industry are to be obtained. I would here impress upon the Minister of Agriculture just as the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) who spoke before me did, the necessity of paying to men trained in agricultural research work salaries commensurate with the importance of that work, and sufficiently high to prevent Canadian universities and other countries taking those experts away. If the regulations of the Civil Service Commission prevent the payment of adequate salaries, means must be found to overcome that limitation, because investigation of the rust problem is a question of national importance. The rust epidemic strikes at the basic industry of Canada, the industry which is the very foundation of Canada's prosperity. Agriculture is by far the most important industry in this country, and unless it is prosperous no other industry can hope to succeed. In order to bear out that contention may I quote from a speech delivered by Daniel Webster at a meeting of farmers in Boston .in 1840. On that occasion that distinguished statesman said:
Agriculture feeds us; to a great degree it clothes us; without it, we could not have manufactures, and we should not have commerce. These all stand together, but they stand together, like pillars in a cluster, the largest in the centre, and the largest is agriculture. Let us remember, too, that we live in a country of small farms, and free-hold tenements; a country, in which men cultivate with their own hands, their own fee-simple acres; drawing not only their subsistence, but also their spirit of independence, and manly freedom from the ground they plough. They are at once its owners, its cultivators, and its defenders. And whatever else may be undervalued, or overlooked, let us never forget that the cultivation of the earth is the most important labour of man.
Man may be civilized, in some degree, without great progress in manufactures, and with little commerce with his distant neighbours, but without the cultivation of the earth, he is m all countries, a savage. Until he steps from the chase, and fixes himself in some place, and seeks a living from the earth, he is a roaming barbarian. When tillage begins, other arts follow. The farmers, therefore, are the founders of human civilization.
To show the importance of agriculture in our country, let me say that the Canadian Review for 1926-27 gives the gross wealth of Canada's great primary industry of agriculture as approximately $7,817,718,000 for the year 1926. The figures from the same source

for the value of the total production of agriculture are $1,668,175,000, while from forests the total value of production for the same period was $209,276,561; from mines, $241,245,898, and from fisheries, $56,300,633, or a total value from forest, mines and fisheries for the year 1926 of $506,883,092. It will thus be seen that agriculture, with a total production value of $1,668,175,000 for 1926, and forest., mines and fisheries combined, with a total production value of $506,883,092, has to its credit a total production value of $1,161,292,000 in excess of the other three sources of wealth combined.
It is too much for the producers in an industry, which produces $1,121,447,000 value of field crops in a single year and which is being menaced by the scourge of rust until it is in danger of total extinction, to ask that the prosecution of research work along the lines of finding and developing rust-resistant varieties of grain should be carried on vigorously and no expense spared in the prosecution of the work? What has already been spenit upon rust research work has brought excellent results, but it is only a drop in the bucket compared with what will have to be spent by the Minister of Agriculture and hiis associates if success in dealing with the rust question is going to crown their efforts.
I wish to say a word on the Hudson Bay railway question. For the past forty years or more this Hudson Bay railway 'has been a live question in Canada around election time, but I am pleased to see by the speech from the throne that work is proceeding rapidly towards the completion of the railway. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Railways upon the energetic manner in which he carried out the work of selecting a terminal for the railway and also upon his prompt decision that Churchill was the better of the two ports in question. I have carefully studied the Palmer report upon both Nelson and Churchill, and from the data contained therein I have no difficulty in arriving at the conclusion that Churchill is by far the better ocean terminal for the Hudson Bay railway, and the wonder is that it was not selected years ago.
In conjunction with what the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) has said, I wish to say a few words about highway construction in Canada. A few years ago the federal authorities voted a lump sum of money which was paid over to the different provinces for highway construction upon the basis of population. I think the Dominion government was prepared to pay one-third of the construction costs up to a certain limit per mile.

The Address-Mr. Lovie
but my information is that that money is all expended. As the provincial governments of the prairie provinces are embarking upon quite an extensive program of highway construction, something which is long overdue, I would ask the Dominion authorities to vote this session a substantial sum of money to be paid over to the different provinces upon a mileage basis, to assist in the construction of all-weather roads.
Regarding the tariff, let me say right here that Manitoba members, in common with all members from the prairie provinces, are pledged to insist upon and support a policy of tariff reduction. Everyone living between the Red river and the Rocky mountains is opposed to a tariff higher than is necessary to produce sufficient revenue to run the affairs of government. They realize that a high tariff is an injustice because it allows one class of people in a country to levy toll upon the other classes; in other words, to levy taxes upon their neighbours for their own special benefit. From the commencement of the session of 1922 until the close of the session of 1926 protection of Canadian industries and still higher protection was steadily preached in season and out of season from the Conservative side of the house. Not a word was said about the agriculturists in western Canada, a class who, by no stretch of the imagination, can derive any benefit from a protective tariff, but who can be badly hampered in their operations by the enhanced cost of living and production caused by protection. Canada which is raising around 400,000,000 bushels of wheat per annum has to find an export market for a large part of that commodity as well as for other agricultural products, and upon all products of which a portion is exported, the export price sets the price for home consumption.
Because Canada is an exporting country she requires to have a very low tariff to enable trade to flow freely across her boundaries. No nation can export its surplus commodities unless it is prepared to import at the same time, and no nation can purchase the surplus products of another without paying for them in goods. International trade is not carried on with gold as a medium of settlement, but goods pay for goods to the mutual benefit of both parties to the transaction. Before last session the tariff advisory board had only been a short time at work, and consequently the Finance minister did1 not feel justified in making tariff reductions as the evidence in none of the cases submitted to the board was completed. But now that the evidence is completed in a good many cases
that have come before the board, the consumers in the country as a body are looking forward to tariff reduction during this session of parliament. In the matter of the cotton tariff schedule which was argued before the tariff board, the evidence brought out the fact that Canadian consumers of cotton paid for their requirements in cotton $19,000,000 above import value. The Canadian people paid $19,000,000 partly in taxes and partly in higher prices to keep this industry in Canada. In spite of that the cotton manufacturers had an application before the tariff board for an increase in the duties on cotton, but they certainly have not established any claim for higher duties unless it be on the assumption that they wish to be regarded as recipients of compassionate grants from the Canadian people.
One word now about immigration and I have finished. The speech from the throne mentions immigration and I would just say this, that it is something very strange if Canada, with its far-flung territory and vast resources, with a population of three persons to the square mile, while the United States has a population of thirty-five to the square mile, cannot support a population of more than nine or ten million people such as we have at present. We must take a broad view of the immigration question. Canada can support twenty million of a population just as easily as she supports half that number now, and were there that many in Canada, all settled and doing well, Canada would be more prosperous than she is at present.
Criticism is being levelled at the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) by some for bringing immigrants into the country, and by others for not bringing in a sufficient number; and almost everyone thinks he could run the Department of Immigration a good deal better than it is being run; but if he had a try at it for a year he would find that in spite of the most rigid selection of immigrants that could be practised, misfits would get into the country and cause trouble. I commend the scheme which the minister mentioned that he had in view of bringing boys from the old land, from good homes, and giving them a year's training in agriculture in Canada under the supervision of the Department of Immigration. They certainly will not all make farmers: it is not to be expected they will, but there is no reason why they will not make good citizens and take to the ways of the land of their adoption very quickly. That the years from fourteen to eighteen i3 a very good age for a boy to emigrate, I can attest to from personal experience, as it was
Ministers oj the Crown

when I was sixteen years of age that I crossed the Atlantic as an immigrant and made Canada my home, a choice, Mr. Speaker, which as the years have rolled past, I have seen no reason to regret.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, February 9, 1928
The house -met at three o'clock.

subtopic: BILL TO OBVIATE NECESSITY OF RE-ELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE

speechtext: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (Cartier) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 28, to remove the necessity of the re-election of members of the House of Commons of Canada on acceptance of office.

subtopic: BILL TO OBVIATE NECESSITY OF RE-ELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: BILL TO OBVIATE NECESSITY OF RE-ELECTION UPON ACCEPTANCE OF OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of introducing this bill last year, but it failed to be enacted into law owing to the *somewhat precipitate prorogation of parliament. I am introducing it again in the hope that it may be passed this year. The bill is similar in its provisions to the measure which was enacted in 1926 by the British parliament, and since that time by certain of the states of the Commonwealth of Australia and the Dominion of New Zealand. Its purpose is set forth in one paragraph, to the effect that a member of parliament on attaining cabinet rank is not obliged to submit himself to his constituents for re-election. I think this provision will appeal to many in this house, to those who are on the front benches as well as to those who hope to be.
For the information of the house I may say that the statute was passed by the British House of Commons on the 15th July, 1926. It became law in New South Wales in 1906, and was also passed in the state of Tasmania and the Dominion of New Zealand. In some of the other states it has not yet been enacted into law. I shall have something further to say when the bill is read a second time.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. S. W. JACOBS (Cartier) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 29, to amend the Railway Act (Return tickets).

Explain.
[Mr. Lovie.J

Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of introducing this bill, or one similar to it, on several previous occasions. It was strongly opposed by the two railway companies, which makes me believe that it must be for the benefit of the people. The bill is copied from the act which is in force in England, and its provisions are to be found in the one section which reads as follows:
A return ticket issued by any railway company between any two points in Canada shall be accepted by any other railway company whose line runs between the same terminals.
I introduced the bill first in the parliament of 1922. I think it was introduced subsequently, but it had some rough sledding and did not emerge from the railway committee. The intellectual calibre of the present parliament being so much higher than that of previous parliaments I hope the measure will be enacted into law this session.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
The house resumed from Wednesday, February 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to resume the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, may I be permitted to join with hon. members who have preceded me, not in offering a dose of soapy, tepid water, to quote the words of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), but rather in sincerely congratulating the hon. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley), who so ably moved the address and the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) who so ably seconded it. Both of these hon. gentlemen acquitted themselves very creditably when you consider the poor material which was placed at their disposal.
Before proceeding further I want to draw to the attention of hon. members a very discourteous retort made to me by the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) during the course of his address yesterday. The hon. gentleman was telling the house how well the recommendations of the Duncan report had been implemented by this government, and he was quoting figures to show that on some commodities an excess of twenty per cent reduction had been made. Having in mind the words of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) when he referred to bread and

The Address

Mr. Quinn
butter and jam being handed out by the premier of Quebec to one of his political favourites, the Postmaster General used that term, and during his address I interjected the remark:
You will add jam to the bread and butter.
The reply of that hon. gentleman was:
It would be better if the hon. gentleman would add some sense to his interjections.
I did not make the remark in an offensive way; I consider it was very appropriate to the occasion, and I resent the implication of the Postmaster General that there was no sense in the remark. I leave it to the decision of hon. members if there was not as much sense in my interjection as there was in the whole speech of the Postmaster General.
While I am dealing with that hon. gentleman, may I bring another matter to the attention of the house? This is what he said in his speech yesterday:
Let me call the attention of the hon. senior member for the city of St. John to a statement which he made yesterday and which is not in accordance with the facts. The hon. gentleman, if I mistake not-and if I am wrong 1 know he will correct me-stated that the Canadian National Railways had submitted a freight schedule to the railway commission and that the railway commission had returned it to them -with orders to revise their schedule to give a 20 per cent reduction. I want to say now-and I am not saying this in contradiction of the hon. gentleman personally because I believe that he was misinformed and got this so-called information through the instrumentality of the St. John board of trade -that that statement is absolutely false. I make that statement boldly because within ten minutes after the hon. gentleman made his statement on the floor of this house, I called up the railway commission and quoted him verbatim and in reply the railway commission said, No.
Let me read a letter from the secretary of the Board of Railway Commissioners under date of July 30, 1927.
Alistair Fraser, Esq., K.C.,
Commission Counsel,
Canadian National Railways,
Montreal.
Dear Sir,

Referring to this matter, I am instructed to say that at a late meeting of the board consideration was given to the tariffs filed by your company under the authority of the Maritime Rates Act, and that the rates shown in such tariffs are inconsistent with provisions of the act and cannot be approved by the board; also that your company is directed to file forthwith, in place of the tariffs so already filed by it and not approved, such tariffs as are required by section (3) of the said act showing a reduction of approximately twenty per cent below the tolls or rates existing on the first of July, 1927.
That is the answer to my hon. friend, and I will leave it to the judgment of the house how much consideration can be given to statements made by him.
I will proceed to deal with the address of the hon. member for Hants-Kings who said:
Canada is prospering; we no longer talk of being on the eve of prosperity; we are enjoying prosperity. That prosperity has been briefly mentioned in the speech from the throne, and is more fully dealt with in the reports or addresses which have been presented by the presidents and general managers of the great Canadian banks to their shareholders during the last few weeks. These addresses tell the story of a greater progress than has ever before been experienced in the history of Canada, a greater prosperity than Canada has ever enjoyed.
I may say to the hon. member for Hants-Kings that the progress of any country cannot be measured by the success of its banking, financial and brokerage institutions. I recall at the end of last year reading in the [DOT] press of my native city of Halifax that a certain brokerage firm had granted a bonus of two hundred per cent to all its employees. Is that an indication of prosperity? Of course it is of brokerage firms and financial institutions; but I ask my hon. friend from Nova Scotia: Did that apply to the farmers, the people engaged in agricultural pursuits in his province? Did that apply to the fishermen of the maritime provinces? Did it apply to the miners and men engaged in other labouring pursuits? He knows the answer and the house knows it. So we cannot judge as to the prosperity of this country by the success of our banking and financial institutions. Further on in his speech the hon. member said:
... a very real reason for the tardiness on the part of the maritime provinces to share in the prosperity of Canada. That cause is the lack of markets for agricultural products in that part of the Dominion.
The hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Mac-Nutt) pointed out very clearly how that applied to the dairymen of Nova Scotia and how the government have in their own hands the remedy with regard to the dairymen of that province. I ask: Does it apply to the farmers, for instance, to the producers of potatoes? May I suggest to the hon. member for Hants-Kings, who comes from a potato-growing district, that if he is looking for wider markets he should go to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), because a market is to be found in his department. Last summer while the Hudson Bay expedition was being equipped they paid 812.50 a
The Address-Mr. Quinn

barrel for potatoes from South Carolina to go to Hudson bay. There is a wider market for the hon. member.
As has been pointed out very ably by the representatives of the island of Cape Breton, there is great distress among the coal miners there, and when this same Hudson Bay expedition was being outfitted, all their boats and the supplies for Hudson Bay, all their coal supplies came from the United States.

My hon. friend is
absolutely and completely wrong.
I can bring the proof of it. I have not got it under my hand, but I can bring it.
That all the supplies-
Coal supplies, I said.

Again I state that that
statement is absolutely false.

I think the minister
should withdraw that statement, Mr. Speaker. I raise the point of order.

I would ask the hon.
gentleman not to use that expression. It is rather harsh.
Withdraw!
Am I instructed to withdraw it, Mr. Speaker?

I think it would be
better, to set an example to the house.

I shall endeavour to
keep in order, Mr. Speaker, but the statement of the hon. gentleman is certainly not in accordance with the facts.

Then, Mr. Speaker, I will
ask to have the report tabled in this house regarding the purchase of supplies for the Hudson Bay expedition.

You will certainly get
it.

The hon. member for Hants-Kings also said in his address:
In addition to that, the production in many lines of agricultural endeavour has increased quite considerably. There is also a revival of interest in mining in Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces as well, which in itself is very promising.
I notice that the hon. member did not mention where credit was due for the increased production in many lines of agriculture in his native province. That credit is due, Mr. Speaker, to the present administration in Nova Scotia which has seen fit to

appoint a department of natural resources, administered by a competent head, under which there has been a great increase in agricultural production in Nova Scotia in the last two years. If my hon. friend is honest, and I am sure he is, he will give full credit to the Department of Natural Resources of Nova Scotia for the wonderful progress that has been made in agriculture in that province; and similarly with regard to the increased activity in mining, which has been due to the splendid administration of the local mines department.
Dealing with the Duncan report the hon. member for Hans-Kings said:
Harbour commissioners have also been appointed for the city of Halifax, and it is hoped that this body will give some degree of direction and unity to the efforts of the people of that city to improve existing conditions.
I have not much to say by way of criticism as to that. We will first give the commission a chance to work. There may be some criticism in another session, but for the present all I wish to say to the Prime Minister and his cabinet in that regard is that if they had given more consideration to the business qualifications than to the political affiliations of the board, a better board might have been secured.
Considerable criticism has been levelled at the Department of Immigration, and justly so. Let me ask the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) if he can justify the dismissal of the caterer of the Immigration department at Halifax other than for political reasons, Oither than for the purpose of appointing a political follower of his own party who was very badly in need of a job. George Foley held that position to his credit and in a way that has won for him. praise from every transportation company operating out of Halifax. There was never a word of complaint, never a criticism about his conduct of the catering of the Immigration department at Halifax, and I tell this house and the minister that he cannot justify the dismissal of that gentleman. When hon. gentlemen talk about the progress and prosperity of Canada, I conclude that the progress they have in mind is to drive every man, woman and child who is not of the same political faith as themselves out of this country to the United States or some other countiy.	.
I am going to bring to the attention of the house a case which perhaps the Minister of Immigration will have an opportunity to explain. It is a case which came under my personal observation. I refer to the Mc-Conachie case. The minister knows the case

The Address-Mr. Quinn
very well. This man McConaehie, a Scotch miner, located in Lanarkshire, Scotland, served all through the great war, was wounded, and treated in hospital in England for a considerable time. Due to post-war conditions, he could not get work in his native country, and he decided to emigrate to Canada. He came out here to Glace Bay and obtained employment, and worked there continually for eighteen months. He has letters of recommendation as to his character, efficiency, and honesty, from the manager of the mines in Glace Bay. He saved his money and made a home so that he could bring out his wife and little family from Scotland. Finally he was able to send for them, and his wife with five little children made preparations to emigrate. First there was a mental and physical examination by the roster doctor in their home. This the family passed successfully. They came to Glasgow, where they had to undergo a similar examination, which they passed successfully. They disposed of all their household effects, and sailed on board the steamship Letitia, where, according to the regulations, the ship's physician again subjected them to an examination, which they passed successfully. They arrived in Halifax in December, about a week before Christmas, where another examination was made by I think Dr. Rutherford, who works in Quebec during the summer months and in Halifax during the winter. That doctor discovered that the infant child of fourteen months was feeble-minded. I have interviewed many medical men of prominence since this case came to my attention, and up to the present time I have failed to find a single physician who would say that a doctor can speak with any degree of certainty as to the mental condition of a 'Child of fourteen months. That family was detained in Halifax in the Immigration department, and eventually the case came to my attention, and I visited the family and made personal observations. Here was a bonny little Scotch woman, virile and strong, with a healthy, red face; as good a specimen of a Scotch woman as you could possibly get, and they are all pretty good. There were five children, ranging in age from eight years down to fourteen months. I went into the immigration office about five o'clock in the evening; the family were sitting there with the father, who had come from Glace'Bay to meet them. When I told them who I was, in company with the immigration chaplain, tears rolled down the cheeks of that father and mother when they told me of their case and how they had been detained there for three weeks. I asked for the story of the McConaehie family, and he showed the baby to me in the arms of its
mother. The baby's back was turned to the father, but when he said "Come, Bunny, come to father," the baby turned around, put out her arms and went to the father. That was the mentally defective child. I did not see any evidence of the Mongolian type to which the department referred in connection with this child. I stood there talking to the father and mother for three or four minutes, while tlhe baby was in the arms of its father. Then the mother turned to the child and called it by name, and it turned and put out its arms and went to its motheT. I went over and chuckled the little kiddie under the chin, and it smiled at me.
Oh, oh.

It could not do otherwise.
I offered it a little candy, and it put out its little hand and took it, and this was the child said to be mentally defective and feebleminded.
What was the position of the Department of Immigration? They said the child must be deported to Scotland, and I suppose that is what my friend the minister calls encouraging British immigration. I wired the minister to this effect:
Strongly protest against deportation MeCona-chie family owing alleged feeble-mindedness child aged one who was examined and passed in Scotland by doctor selected Canadian government. Sailing was approved your department and family broke home. Husband working for and highly recommended by Dominion Coal. Has good home ready. Consider deportation of desirable family criminal and grievous blunder. Strongly urge admittance.
Felix P. Quinn, M.P.
Here is the answer, and hon. members will keep in mind that this child had been examined four times.
Your wire. There is no doubt. . . .
Three doctors said the child was not feebleminded while one said she was, so I submit that this is the judgment of the Minister of Immigration.

I protest against any such statement as the last. The hon. member must know that matters of this kind are dealt with by the Department of Health and not by the Department of Immigration. I have nothing in the world to do with it. [DOT]

This telegram was sent to
Robert J. Forke, Esq., Minister of Immigration, and the reply came back signed by Robert J. Forke, M.P., Minister of Immigration. I realized at the time that it was a case where the understrappers should not be dealt with, and I wanted to deal directly with the minister in charge of that department.
The Address-Mr. Quinn

You have the advantage
just now; that is all I have to say.
Mr. Speaker, just to clear up the point-
Order.
There is no doubt-

I thought the
house would like to have it cleared up.
Order.

This is the reply I received:
Your wire. There is no doubt as to the mental condition McConachie child. She has been definitely certified as feeble-minded with no prospect ever developing to anything near normal. Law specifically prohibits entry to Canada feeble minded persons. Apparent carelessness roster doctor cannot be accepted as grounds for admission prohibited immigrant who will require institutional or other care throughout lifetime. Decision to deport all members family was due to statement of mother that if child not admitted all wished to return. Cannot agree that action of carrying out requirements law is either criminal or grievous blunder. In final analysis Canada is entitled to protection from possible liability lifetime maintenance child. Father subsequently requested that other children be allowed remain with him in Canada and request complied with.
Robert Forke.
Now, sir, I followed that up with a letter under date of January 7, as follows:
Replying to your wire of the 4th instant I have personally investigated the McConachie ease and have seen the infant Margaret, who is alleged to be feeble-minded, and I protest against deportation for the following reasons:
Firstly, there is conflict of medical opinion. Roster doctor certified infant to be mentally and physically fit, and you are aware that roster doctors are selected because of their good standing and are appointed for express purpose of preventing deportations on physical or mental grounds, and therefore their opinions should have great weight.
Secondly, the infant, being only one year old, it is not possible to forecast with any degree of certainty what its future mental condition will be.
_ Thirdly, the board of immigration officers who investigated the case were very favourably impressed with the family.
So was I:
Fourthly, I protest on humane grounds. The husband's father, mother, brother, sisters and all relatives are settled in Nova Scotia and all are. like himself, doing useful work. The mother, on receipt of letter from immigration authorities in England approving of sailing, sold her home, and if now deported would have no home or friends to go to.
Lastly, I consider the deportation under such circumstances criminal, inhuman and a grievous blunder. It is clearly a case to be dealt with under section 4 of the Immigration Act, which was framed not only to safeguard the interests of Canada but to deal with justice to the immigrant as well.

For the above reasons I insist that this family should have admittance to Canada.
Now let me quote section 4 of the Immigration Act:
The minister may issue a written permit authorising any person to enter Canada, or having entered or landed in Canada to remain therein without being subject to the provisions of this act. Such permit shall be in the form A of the schedule to this act, and shall be expressed to be in force for a specified period only, but it may at any time be extended or cancelled by the minister in writing.
McConachie wired to the Minister of Immigration first, asking for a special board of three doctors, the expense of which he was prepared to bear, and by whose decision he was willing to abide, but to that wire he received no reply. When he has a chance I will ask the Minister of Immigration to say why section 4 was not applied in this case, because the mental condition of this infant could not be forecast with any degree of certainty.
Might I reply now?
Order.

The hon. member asked me
to tell him.
Order.

Then I have the final letter
from the minister:
I am in receipt of your letter of the 7th instant, having reference to the case of Margaret McConachie, and have carefully perused the same. You state that there is a conflict of medical opinion, apparently basing the said statement on the grounds that the roster doctor passed the child. Whilst it is true that the roster doctor did not certify the child as being mentally defective, the evidence on file very clearly indicates that had she been properly examined, she would have been so certified. There is no conflict of medical opinion in so far as the medical officers of the Department of Health are concerned; in fact, there is a unanimous opinion on the part of both of these officers who personally examined the child, and their diagnosis was approved of by the chief medical officer of the Department of Health at Ottawa. It would be a most unreasonable attitude to ignore the diagnosis of three experienced Canadian medical officers and accept as establishing mental fitness the fact that a roster doctor had passed the child.
You state that it is not possible to forecast with any degree of certainty what the child's future mental condition will be, in view of the fact that it is now only one year old. I am unable to accept this statement, and my remark on the point in question is based on the statement of the chief officer of the immigration medical service of the Department of Health that "in the present instance (referring to the case of Margaret McConachie) with the physical characteristics of the type described as Mongolian, the mental deficiency is quite inseparable from the physical abnormalities as set out in the history. That conference, representing all the dominions of the empire, unanimously agreed to define their position and mutual relation as autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, while united by common allegiance to the crown and freely associated as members of the British commonwealth of nations.
When my hon. friend the acting leader of the Conservative party, after that conference, undertook to throw cold water on its achievements and charged that it was with a feeling of disloyalty to the crown that Liberals ventured to assert our equal status with the motherland and the .other dominions in their own spheres, he was effectively silenced by Premier Stanley Baldwin of Great Britain, who in Toronto on August 7, 1927, declared:

Again he said:

Mark you, Mr. Speaker, these are all Conservatives, but they are the right kind of Conservatives; these are all big men.

In accepting the popular meaning of that term, with certain mental reservations as to the extent and adequacy of the prosperity indicated, I have no intention of denying its presence. However, I regard the very mention of prosperity in the speech from the throne as being in the nature of an announcement, as though prosperity were not normally to be expected. If prosperity were a normal condition, as it might very well be, there would be no need for any announcement concerning it, but as things are prosperity is fittingly mentioned in the speech from the throne. To me, that amounts to the announcement of a welcome visitor, which comes to us at uncertain intervals, and I am very glad that the government have had notice of his arrival. I rise now not only to welcome that visitor with the government, but to insist that the government shall take at this session of parliament, and at subsequent sessions, steps which will compel that welcome visitor to become a permanent member of our family, if such be possible. In other words, I rise to urge a consideration which may lead to the stabilization of prosperity.
I am very glad to note that the government were too wise to claim that prosperity was coming to Canada through any particular act of theirs. I do not say this in any criticism of the government, I merely wish to indicate that if the government had claimed credit for the announced prosperity they would also have to take the blame for the unemployment and depressions which have characterized our Canadian industrial life for the last ten years, and they would also have to accept the responsibility for the depression and unemployment which will inevitably follow the prosperity which they have now announced.
This indicated prosperity brings us face to face with the chief problem of modern industrial life. Anyone who is at all observant must be convinced that industry and business move in fitful cycles of prosperity, alternating with dreaded cycles of depression. General reflection on this phenomenon has been crystallized into a few very definite opinions which vary, naturally, and which have been frequently expressed in this chamber. These different opinions have been brought forward in this . chamber voluminously during periods of depression and to-day, Mr. Speaker, I wish to review some of these opinions because I anticipate that they will be repeated a few years hence when dealing with the next period of depression. Hon. members who voiced these convictions will probably recognize them, but I draw them to your attention now if for no other reason than to show just how far we are from analyzing in a scientific way the real problem before us, and how much further we are from finding a satisfactory solution thereof.
The first opinion which I wish to recall will be that of the Minister of Finance. I do not, of course, refer to the present Minister of Finance because he may not be in that position when these speeches are next made, but whoever may be the Minister of Finance at that time will take the attitude that neither his department, the financial institutions in general nor the government will accept any responsibility for the unemployment and depression which he will, of course, deplore. His attitude is not hard to picture; "Deus Vult" will be his helpless cry, he will reluctantly admit that unemployment is present, and out of the very sympathy of his human heart he will be sorry for the sufferers, but the only thing he will be able to do will be to give a very small pittance of charity and hope for the return of the tide of prosperity.
Then there is another opinion which we have heard expressed and which we will doubtless hear again, that is that unemployment is caused by men who absolutely refuse to work. No explanation will be given of the fact that these men charged with refusing to work were the men who did work the year before, when prosperity was at its height, and no explanation will be given of tlhe fact that because of their very industry the shelves of the warehouses will be piled1 high with goods which cannot be removed and consumed thus carrying out the very aim of industry itself.

In other words, we are content with the dry as dust excrescences of an old outworn economic theory* which belongs to what is known as the "dismal science." Happily for the future, however, these are not the only opinions. There are those to-day who believe-not as the result of any blind credulity, but by reason of an inevitable conclusion derived from a close scientific analysis of industrial phenomena-that the depression which we have so often deplored is preventable; and if that is so, then those in authority should be held responsible for its recurrence.
What are the facts on which this hopeful belief is based? What are the steps in the analysis that leads to this conclusion? Everyone knows that prosperity comes gradually and finally ends in a boom. The boom slumps and ends in a depression. When prosperity begins naturally everyone in his own interest does the very thing which is needed to bring more prosperity; that is to say, when prosperity begins the psychological element begins to work-manufacturers and other producers of goods increase their means of production, and the money spent in this way increases

the consumers' purchasing power, and on goes the prosperity wave. And if bad times come a similar process is followed. In other words, the individual acts in the way described because he does not expect that the tendency which he has noticed, whether one of depression or of prosperity, can be stopped. He well knows that there is no agency to which he can look for any assistance.
Now, is there a way by which extreme depressions may be avoided? Is there a way by which prosperity may be made permanent? I will summarize briefly the essential factors which suggest the possibility of a stabilized prosperity. First, no one will deny that Canada is well equipped with natural resources, with plant facilities and with man power to increase production ad lib. No one will deny that much of the invested capital in Canada to-day is returning a poor profit, and in some cases is entirely lost, because it has been invested in manufacturing facilities the product of which cannot be purchased. The next thing to be noticed is that the people in Canada actually desire more goods. I refer to the statement of conditions as made by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) on Monday night. She pointed out that a very large percentage of the homes of our rural people could be very much improved, and that these rural people are very anxious to have them improved; that is, they desire more goods and higher standards of living. And undoubtedly it would be well for them if they could get more goods and higher standards of living. Why, in face of the capacity of manufacturing industry to produce plenty, and in the face of their desire for plenty, do they not have plenty?
Let me follow the steps of the reasoning in this regard. They do not have plenty because they do not create plenty; they do not create plenty because plenty cannot be sold. We are not in a position to buy any more than is being now created. More could not be sold if it were produced because consumers do not have sufficient income with which to buy more. The best proof of this is shown in the extensive selling on the instalment plan which has taken place in the last few years. It is estimated that during the past year three billion dollars worth of goods was sold or moved in the United States on the instalment plan. I am not advocating the instalment plan-do not forget that. I think the instalment plan is mathematically impossible, and that some day it must stop. I merely use this fact to indicate that if these people had had the money they would have bought the three billion dollars' worth of

The Address-Mr. Irvine
goods in cash instead of on the instalment plan. It is merely a fact to indicate that if the people had more money they would buy more goods.
Since producers cannot produce any more goods than consumers can consume, and since consumers cannot consume any more goods than they can buy and pay for, it is surely our duty to inquire into the sources of their income. Where do consumers get their money? Well, I think anyone will be ready to answer that consumers generally get their money in the form of wages, dividends, interest, profit and so forth. But the point to be emphasized is that all such moneys come from industry; and industry, on the other hand, has no other source of receiving its money than from the consumer, while the consumer has no other source of receiving purchasing power but from industry. Thus there is a constant circuit flow of money from industry to the consumer, and from the consumer back again to industry. So that if industry does not receive enough money from the consumer to buy its output, then its output cannot be bought out. Similarly, if consumers do not receive sufficient money from industry to pay for the output, it cannot be paid for. If industry therefore paid back to consumers all the money which consumers have sent to industry, and if, on the other hand, consumers could buy goods with all the money they received as wages, dividends, interest, profits, and so forth, from industry, we would have a pretty steady circuit flow; we would be able to buy a fixed volume of goods at a certain level of price.
But these things do not run so smoothly as that. We are living under a profit system, and consequently the man who produces goods must sell them for a price higher than it cost him to produce them. Moreover, it is necessary for corporations and individuals to save, and money that is saved appears first in the production of more goods, so that there is a constant tendency to pile upon the shelf goods that represent a surplus, not above the capacity of consumers to consume, but above the possibility of consumers to pay for with the wages they receive in the process of production. The right flow of money would be that amount which would balance the goods flowing into the market, and it is the lack of an agency to regulate that right flow of money that accounts for the recurrent depression and unemployment against which I am speaking.
But let us ask now, why it is that an agency of this character has not been established, that is to say, an.agency for the pur-56103-20
pose of regulating the proper flow of money into the market. The reason is that orthodox economists, those who wrote their treatises prior to the modern development and prior, to the modern problem, are the accepted authorities, regardless of the fact that their theories are contradicted by facts known to every business man capable of noting a fact. What is that obsolete theory to which those in authority give a blind allegiance? It is the assumption that no agency is required to regulate the flow of money, because, forsooth, John Stuart Mill and Adam Smith have assumed that if producers obtain sufficient money for production, then consumers automatically will obtain sufficient to buy out their production. I want to explode this theory of the orthodox economists.
I will ignite the explosive by asking this question: Why cannot the money expended in production enable the consumers to buy the output? What is the reason? I indicated it a few moments ago but I will discuss it more in detail now. Money expended in production cannot buy the output because, in the first place, we are living under what is known as the profit system. I am not speaking against the profit system-I am merely pointing out a fact: We are living under a profit system and that means that the producer must get more for the goods he sells than it costs him to produce them. No man will go into business on any other condition. No man will do anything that will not yield him something in return, whether it be in the form of material wealth or in the way of satisfaction of a psychological kind. But be that as it may, since the producer has to sell his goods for more than it costs him to produce them where will the extra money come from? The money paid out in production is the only money the consumers have to buy with. Consequently there must remain on the shelves of the warehouse a surplus which represents the difference between the amount of money distributed in the process of production and the selling price of the goods. But that is not the only difficulty. Corporations must save. They have to replenish plant and extend it when necessary and this compels them to put by some reserve. Individuals must also save. It is a very admirable characteristic, we are told, to save money, and I am not arguing against it; it is necessary. But every dollar that the individual saves helps to hasten depression. Money saved usually is turned back into further production. But, you say, the consumer's dollar is bound to be somewhere. Yes; but let me show you where it

The Address-Mr. Irvine

usually is when we want it. Suppose it is in the bank: During the period of depression one thing that the bank finds it very difficult to do is to lend money to anyone, so that the consumer's dollar lies there out of the circuit flow and to that extent it is not functioning. The consumer is denied goods in consequence.
Some hon. members in this house may call me a theorist and on that assumption will disregard my plea. Meanwhile hon. gentlemen are giving their tacit endorsement to a theory which underlies our whole industrial system and to which are chargeable the most spectacular failures of that system; a theory which is proven to be false by every fact relevant to the subject. In further pursuance of my theme, I anticipate a question which some thoughtful member may possibly have in mind at this point. That question is this:	What is the cause of a period of
prosperity, since I have indicated that there is never enough money under the ordinary industrial system in the hands of consumers to buy out production? My answer is that prosperity invariably comes during periods of capital expenditure. This capital expenditure causes prosperity because the money expended in capital facilities immediately finds its place in the market for goods. And this increases the purchasing power of the consumer for the reason that, as yet, no goods have come from the facilities in question to balance the amount of money expended, as I have indicated. In this way capital expenditure always helps purchasing power. Let me illustrate this point. Suppose we have in this city a large boot and shoe factory and a period of depression is gradually closing in upon us. The shelves are being crowded with goods which cannot be sold. When the depression is beginning to settle on the factory, when they are paying off their hands, let us assume that the construction of a huge two million dollar plant-say for hydro electric purposes-is undertaken. Immediately construction work begins money is paid out in wages and so forth. But that plant so far has produced no goods to go on the market, it is distributing $2,000,000 of money which is available for the purchase of some of the boots which have been lying on the shelves of the boot and shoe factory which I have supposed. I might cite many instances, such as for example the marked development of the automobile business in the United States. That was a new industry a few short years ago whereas to-day it is chief in volume of production among the industries of the United States. The automobile industry on the other side produced [Air. Irvine.]
last year seven-eighths of the world's output, and in cars and car supplies there was spent in that country six billion dollars. United States prosperity in the last ten years, as compared with the poverty or lack of prosperity in other countries, has been due in large part to this expenditure in automobiles, but this has been so only because the automobile industry has been a growing one. A stabilized industry will not increase the purchasing power of the people because it does not enlarge plant equipment to the same extent as a new industry.
All periods of prosperity are caused by capital expenditure in the manner I have set forth. But just as soon as the goods begin to flow to the market from the new capital facilities, depression sets in and continues until conditions warrant the repeating of the process. In other words, we are prosperous when all the money expended on future production, together with all expended on current production, enables us to buy all the goods available. The position may be made even more clear when I say that in order to be able to buy the output of capital facilities now in use we must build new ones, and in order to buy the output of the new ones we must build still more new ones. When we stop this process disaster immediately overtakes us.
There can be only one solution to this problem, no matter how brought about, and that is our people must in some way be enabled to buy and pay for as much as they can produce of consumers' goods or the full equivalent in the product of other countries. That is to say: There must be sufficient money in the hands of consumers, together with our imports, to balance our industrial output. Someone will ask, why can we not ship our surplus to foreign countries? We can; but if you have not enough money to buy the surplus which you have at home you have not enough with which to buy the imports which, in the proper course of business, should be exchanged for exports. No country is unwise enough to ship goods out without having an equivalent in imports, and what is the use of getting imports without having money with which to pay for them.
I propose now to devote the remaining portion of my remarks to making a few suggestions with a view to the stabilization of the prosperity which is now beginning to make itself felt throughout the country,- suggestions which I shall direct not only to the government but to parliament. I may be mistaken in my estimation of the power of parliament. But at present I regard parliament as being-greater in authority than

In finding a remedy for the present state of affairs in this regard, the first step is to discover something which at present nobody knows, and yet to discover which is well within the range of human intelligence. And how much of that amount is now furnished by the producers of goods in the form of payment for services? I propose, Mr. Speaker, that we set up a federal board which shall collect from every available source: (1) Such information and such data as are required to indicate the correct amount of the consumer's income; (2) With such information in their possession the board would next advise the government how its fiscal policy should be guided in respect to such information; (3) The board shall also determine the exact time at which public expenditures undertaken by the government shall be launched, the manner of its financing, and the extent to which it shall be put within a given time. In times of prosperity the government could shorten up its public works program, while it would extend that program in order to stem a tendency towards depression. In this way the control of money in proper relation to production would be possible. I should like to explain this more fully, but time will not permit.

ment. I suggest, sir, that this government should organize such a board as I have indicated which board both by its own acts, and by the data which it will be in a position to furnish, will be enabled to give leadership to business in general. do they amount to when they are examined? The other day I heard an hon. member from Nova Scotia state that he had a national coal policy to announce for the benefit of Canada.
I prepared myself to listen to him with great interest, because we have a very serious coal problem in British Columbia; but the hon. gentleman had not got into his stride before it developed that his idea of a national coal policy was purely a selfish provincial policy, asking for an increased tariff for the benefit of Nova Scotia alone. Notwithstanding the fact that he was aware-and he must have been aware, because I told him so last year and, I think, the session before-that if his object was attained of an increased duty of one dollar a ton on bituminous coal imported into Canada, that would mean the ruin of our coal mines in British Columbia because our market is largely in the United States and as we have a reciprocal duty with the United States it would mean that their duty would also be increased a dollar a ton-notwithstanding this he elaborated his view, under the guise of a national coal policy, that we should have a largely increased duty on coal. That, however, was not so remarkable except that his attitude was purely provincial, selfish and narrow; but it was not so illogical in one way because he belongs to a party which believes in the principle of tariffs and still higher tariffs as a remedy for all ills.
But what shall be said when we come to the suggested coal policy of the other end of Canada, that put forward by the press in a very expansive way and by some of the members from Alberta? Their idea of a national coal policy appears to be that this house shall impose upon the two railway companies of Canada a statutory rate vastly below what the coal can be economically carried at. Sir Henry Thornton has the credit of being a capable administrator, and that has been well demonstrated. If he could carry this coal at a rate that would be ever so slightly profitable to him there is no question that, owing to the volume of it, he would be very anxious to carry it. The fact that he has turned it down and cannot meet the wishes of hon. members from Alberta is proof that the statutory rate asked, no matter how it may be camouflaged, is an attempt to put into effect a rate that Sir Henry Thornton and the Canadian Pacific cannot economically maintain. That is the full and absolute and only meaning that can be taken out of this demand for a statutory rate. If I were to talk in the langugae of the man on the street and not in the language of this parliament I would say, perhaps, that that smacks strongly of what is popularly
known as "graft", if we accept the meaning of graft-taking from many people either money or privileges for the benefit of a few people, because that is what is proposed in this case. This comes with particularly bad grace from hon. members who, a few years ago, could not find it in their hearts to protect the children and the dairy farmers of Canada by voting against the encouragement and manufacture of oleomargarine. Of course I refuse to no one the right to change his mind on principles if he sees fit to do so. I only mention this in passing and drop a flower on the grave of political consistency.
As I have said, I have no objection to the principle of protection. As hon. members have perhaps heard me say before, I have no political morals on the question of tariffs, and I would cheerfully advocate protection to-day if I thought it was for the benefit of my province or district, or free trade tomorrow. I do not believe it is a matter of religious belief that should be adhered to, and this saves me from getting into many an awkward position. If this desire for assistance in regard to coal mined in Alberta were put into the form of a bonus-because that is the least vicious form of protection there is, and is far preferable to a tariff-I would have no great objection; but I have a strong objection to its being camouflaged as a rate at the expense of our national railways, because this means the undermining of the whole system, expensively built up, of our government owned railway. Where is this thing going to stop? Because you cannot give to one man and deny another. If Nova Scotia gets its rate rake-off and Alberta gets its handout, who is to be the next, and where is this principle going to stop?
There is another phase of the matter that attracts my attention as a representative from British Columbia, and more particularly from the coal mining sections of that province. If the coal mines of Alberta have to be pap-fed to-day by a rate east, how long will it be before they will want to be wet-nursed on a rate west into Vancouver? The one would logically, undeniably, follow the other, and where then would our coal mines on Vancouver island come in? They are struggling very hard at present against the competition of fuel oil, and it would obviously be unjust to saddle them with the burden of an unfairly reduced rate from Alberta, of which they would have to pay a portion, in order to ruin their own industry. We have a coal problem in British Columbia, and we have not come whining to this house about it and asking to be pap-fed. Our coal mines are deep, they
The Address-Mr. Neill

are expensive to work, and we are losing our market to American fuel oil. I investigated this question on one occasion with a view to seeing whether we could not find an outlet by shipping our coal, which is on the seaboard, by means of the government merchant marine ships to Montreal or Toronto via the Panama canal, and I have reason to believe that the same reduction that is asked to be given on Alberta coal, which means a present of two dollars a ton, if given on British Columbia coal going to Montreal or Toronto via the Panama canal, might enable our coal carried by the government merchant marine ships to compete in the coal markets of Montreal and Toronto. But we have not asked that, because we did not think it sound policy that we should come here and ask for our profits to be boosted or our business to be supported by the other parts of Canada, especially when it would mean involving the Canadian government railways and the allied merchant marine in a rate that would be economically unsound and bound to lead to heavy deficits. Once you start that principle, where are you going to stop?
I shall not detain the house further, Mr. Speaker, because I understand it is the wish to get through by eleven.
I did not have the advantage of hearing the remarks of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), and I do not know what coal policy he referred to or what his views will be, but I earnestly hope, if the government thinks it necessary to give a subsidy in connection with Alberta coal, that the money will be voted in the estimates as a straight bonus to that industry, and only on coal going easit, and not mixed up or camouflaged with a rate on the railway which will be disastrous to our Canadian National Railways.
Motion (Mr. Ilsley) agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, seconded by Mr. Robb, it was ordered that the address be engrossed and transmitted to His Excellency the Governor General by such members of the house as are of the honourable the Privy Council.

A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1929, was presented by Hon. J. A. Robb (Minister of Finance), read by Mr. Speaker to the house, and referred to the committee of supply.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King, the house proceeded to government notices of motions.

subtopic: PUBLIC PRINTING AND STATIONERY ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Public Printing and Stationery Aet in relation to advances authorized to be made to the king's printer for the purchase of materials, to execute orders and requisitions and payment of wages, and to provide that the total amount of such advances shall at no time exceed the sum of seven hundred thousand dollars or such sum as may hereafter be determined, from time to time, by the governor in council.
He said:	His Excellency the Governor
General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to provide for the disposition and allotment of the canteen funds which were accumulated during the war by certain units of the Canadian Expeditionary Force in Canada, the Canadian Siberian Forces and by the forces stationed at St. Lucia (British West Indies), resulting from the profits of canteens and other like institutions operated by the several units and formations, and for the administration of the same by the provincial board of trustees appointed under the Canteen Funds Act, chapter 34 of the statutes of 1925.
He said:	His Excellency the Governor
General, having been made acquainted with

the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Minister of Finance be authorized to pay to the National Battlefields Commission the sum of seventy-five thousand dollars a year for a period not exceeding ten years from the first day of April, 1928, to be expended by the commission for the purposes of and subject to the provisions of the Act respecting the National Battlefields at Quebec.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the governor in council be authorized to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act such sum or sums of money as may be required, not to exceed in the whole the sum of five hundred million dollars, for paying or redeeming the whole or any portion of loans or obligations of Canada and for purchasing and withdrawing from circulation unmatured securities of Canada; the principal and interest to be charged upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That the Dominion Notes Act be amended to provide that the governor in council may establish branch offices of the Department of Finance for the redemption of Dominion notes (in addition to those already authorized), at such other place or places in Canada as the governor m council, on the recommendation of the treasury board, may authorize.
He said: His Excellency the Governor General, having been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, recommends it to the favourable consideration of the house.
Motion agreed to.

Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved that the house go into committee at the next sitting to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend and revise the Electricity Inspection Act to bring it into conformity with the existing conditions in electricity, in regard to the commercial unit of supply, the units of electrical measure, inspection standards, the verification of meters, and other related matters, and to provide for the appointment of a director and such assistants as may be deemed necessary.
Motion agreed to.
